questions.q: A Hadith promises God’s love to those who meet one another for His sake. What does the editorial say of meeting online when people cannot gather in person?
options: It should be avoided where possible
Not quite. The article says: It too counts as gathering for God’s sake, if it serves the same purpose.
It has no value compared with meeting in person
Not quite. The article says: It too counts as gathering for God’s sake, if it serves the same purpose.
It counts only for the young
Not quite. The article says: It too counts as gathering for God’s sake, if it serves the same purpose.
It too counts as gathering for God’s sake, if it serves the same purpose
Yes. A modern substitute for companionship.
questions.rationale: “A virtual meeting too—if it is for a mission—is to love for the sake of God, and to gather for the sake of God.”

questions.article: The Letter and Spirit of Eid Al-Adha
questions.q: When Abraham told his son of the dream in which he was asked to sacrifice him, how did the son answer?
options: “Father, wait until I am older”
Not quite. The article says: “O my father, do as you are commanded; and God willing, you will find me steadfast”.
“Father, such a dream cannot be true”
Not quite. The article says: “O my father, do as you are commanded; and God willing, you will find me steadfast”.
“Father, let us ask others first”
Not quite. The article says: “O my father, do as you are commanded; and God willing, you will find me steadfast”.
“O my father, do as you are commanded; and God willing, you will find me steadfast”
Right. A ram was then sent in his place.
questions.rationale: “O my father, do as you are commanded; and God willing, you will find me steadfast.”

questions.article: The Letter and Spirit of Eid Al-Adha
questions.q: What spirit does the article say the festival of sacrifice asks believers to renew?
options: Pride in the size of one’s offering
Not quite. The article says: Readiness to give up what is dear for God’s sake: “my prayers, my sacrifice, my life and my death all belong to God”.
The pleasure of a public holiday
Not quite. The article says: Readiness to give up what is dear for God’s sake: “my prayers, my sacrifice, my life and my death all belong to God”.
Readiness to give up what is dear for God’s sake: “my prayers, my sacrifice, my life and my death all belong to God”
Well read. The form recalls the meaning.
A wish to outdo one’s neighbours
Not quite. The article says: Readiness to give up what is dear for God’s sake: “my prayers, my sacrifice, my life and my death all belong to God”.
questions.rationale: “Believers reaffirm their belief in God and pledge themselves to parting with their precious belongings, if there is a need for it.”

questions.q: What does the article call the ideal form of religion?
options: Neither, but philosophy
Not quite. The article says: Ritual and inner spirit going hand in hand, each with its own value.
Spirit alone, with no outward form
Not quite. The article says: Ritual and inner spirit going hand in hand, each with its own value.
Ritual and inner spirit going hand in hand, each with its own value
Yes. Form gives the spirit expression and identity.
Ritual alone, performed exactly
Not quite. The article says: Ritual and inner spirit going hand in hand, each with its own value.
questions.rationale: “One is that in which spirit and rituals (or form) both have their distinct values. That is the ideal version of religion.”

questions.q: A reviewer found two scientific books on bereavement “useful but not elevating.” What does the article say can truly console the bereaved?
options: Avoiding all thought of the dead
Not quite. The article says: Knowing that death begins the real life, and that everything belongs to God.
Knowing that death begins the real life, and that everything belongs to God
Correct. “What is there to lose and lament?”
More detailed medical knowledge
Not quite. The article says: Knowing that death begins the real life, and that everything belongs to God.
Keeping busy with work
Not quite. The article says: Knowing that death begins the real life, and that everything belongs to God.
questions.rationale: “It is only by realizing that death—far from being the end of life—is the beginning of real life that we can begin to cope with the distress and suffering that death leaves in its wake.”

questions.q: The Prophet used to tell a sick person that the illness would be a means of purification. How does the article explain this?
options: Illness is a reward in itself
Not quite. The article says: Illness reveals one’s weakness, removes pride, and turns the heart to God in prayer.
Illness cancels all duties
Not quite. The article says: Illness reveals one’s weakness, removes pride, and turns the heart to God in prayer.
Illness cleanses the body of impurities
Not quite. The article says: Illness reveals one’s weakness, removes pride, and turns the heart to God in prayer.
Illness reveals one’s weakness, removes pride, and turns the heart to God in prayer
Well reasoned. Unbroken ease can make one insensitive.
questions.rationale: “When a sensitive person is afflicted with disease or loss, he discovers his weakness… the disease draws him away from other things and brings him closer to God.”

questions.q: To what does the article compare the difficulties of this world, and what are they for?
options: Walls – to stop him going anywhere
Not quite. The article says: Speed breakers – so that man does not take this world for the real, final one.
Speed breakers – so that man does not take this world for the real, final one
Right. They turn his thinking towards the Hereafter.
Storms – to test his house
Not quite. The article says: Speed breakers – so that man does not take this world for the real, final one.
Debts – to be paid off one by one
Not quite. The article says: Speed breakers – so that man does not take this world for the real, final one.
questions.rationale: “These problems act as speed breakers for human beings. These problems exist so that man does not consider the present world as the real world.”

questions.q: Even the most brilliant people leave the world with much undone. When, according to the article, does life begin to make sense?
options: When one achieves fame
Not quite. The article says: When one accepts that there is a life after death.
When one stops asking such questions
Not quite. The article says: When one accepts that there is a life after death.
When one accepts that there is a life after death
Yes. Then everything falls into place.
When one lives to a great age
Not quite. The article says: When one accepts that there is a life after death.
questions.rationale: “It is only after we accept that there is a life after death, an eternal existence, that we see some meaning in life.”

questions.q: Some say modern civilization has made religion out of date. How does the article answer?
options: New comforts and machines change the outward forms of life, but religion deals with its lasting values, which they do not touch
Exactly. A faster vehicle does not alter right and wrong.
Modern life has no values at all
Not quite. The article says: New comforts and machines change the outward forms of life, but religion deals with its lasting values, which they do not touch.
Religion matters only in villages
Not quite. The article says: New comforts and machines change the outward forms of life, but religion deals with its lasting values, which they do not touch.
Religion must reject modern inventions
Not quite. The article says: New comforts and machines change the outward forms of life, but religion deals with its lasting values, which they do not touch.
questions.rationale: “The relevance of religion is its concern with fundamental values rather than with social manifestations. Social phenomena undergo constant changes, whereas the values of life are immutable.”

questions.q: A widow of another faith asked Caliph Umar for help; he offered her his faith and she declined. What did he do?
options: Sent her to another official
Not quite. The article says: Gave her more than she had asked, and prayed, “O God, bear witness that I have not exercised any coercion”.
Gave her more than she had asked, and prayed, “O God, bear witness that I have not exercised any coercion”
Well read. “There shall be no compulsion in religion.”
Asked her to think again and return
Not quite. The article says: Gave her more than she had asked, and prayed, “O God, bear witness that I have not exercised any coercion”.
Withdrew his offer of help
Not quite. The article says: Gave her more than she had asked, and prayed, “O God, bear witness that I have not exercised any coercion”.
questions.rationale: “Umar then gave her more than she had asked for… ‘O God, bear witness that I have not exercised any coercion on this lady.’”
